pr_title: Make Process.WaitForExitAsync wait for redirected output reads
pr_body:
Addresses an issue where Process.WaitForExitAsync doesn't wait for background redirected output reads, a behaviour which diverges from the sync method equivalent. Fixes #42556.

cc @adamsitnik @stephentoub

comments:

I can reproduce the issue on both Windows and Linux (i.e. the test you provided passes on both platforms)

Please, take this fix to 5.0 release.
process.WaitForExitAsync is new and very handful api
I don't think we could justify backporting the fix to 5.0 this late into the release cc @jeffhandley

I would also support backporting this fix to .NET 5. When people update their code to use async methods, they don't expect to introduce potential bugs in their code. This one is not frequent, but it did occur a few times in my case. Also, some analyzers may detect async equivalent methods and suggest refactoring. By applying the change, you'll introduce a bug in your project.

If this fix is not backported, please consider adding a remark to indicate you need to call WaitForExit after to wait for redirected ouput stream.

Once the fix is completed, merged, and tested, we can evaluate it against the .NET 5.0 GA bar.  With there being a workaround and having the opportunity to mention the workaround in API docs, it's unlikely that it'll meet the bar though.

review_comments: Is it possible this might throw?  If so, is that the exception we want to bubble up rather than the one being handled here?

> Is it possible this might throw?

It seems like it can.

> If so, is that the exception we want to bubble up rather than the one being handled here?

I think so, the comments seem to indicate that the handled exception should not be surfaced if the process has exited. At the same time, it makes sense to bubble up any exceptions thrown by the wait method.

@stephentoub I chose to copy the `TaskTimeoutExtensions.cs` instead of moving the file from the `Common/tests` folder, since I really only need this one method.

Would probably make sense to add a few unit tests for that?
It's strange we're now using two different "with cancellation" waiting approaches in the same body of code.
I noticed that as well. While there are similarities I don't think we should combine the two approaches.
